dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Good morning, Residential Services. How can I help?

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Hi. I live in Building C of Rattana Hall, room 412. I'm here about a leak in my bathroom ceiling. I reported it online ten days ago, but nobody has come.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Let me look up your request. Ah, here it is. It was marked as low priority because the form said 'minor drip'.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: It was minor when I filled in the form. Now there's water running down the wall, and a brown stain is spreading across the ceiling.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: That changes things. Water near the walls can reach the electrical wiring, so I'm upgrading it to urgent. A technician should be there by this afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Thank you. Will I need to be in the room?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Not necessarily. If you sign this permission slip, the technician can let himself in with a master key.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: I'd rather be there, actually. My laptop and all my lecture notes are on the desk right under the stain.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: Understandable. Then I'd move anything valuable away from that corner right away, just in case.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Good idea. And if the repair takes several days, is there anywhere else I could stay?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: We keep a few guest rooms in Building A for situations like this. If the technician decides the bathroom can't be used, come back here and we'll sort out a temporary room for you.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: That's a relief. Should I update my online request as well?

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.text: No need. I've added a note myself. But next time a problem gets worse, call us instead of waiting. The online system doesn't alert anyone when a request changes.

dialogue.speaker: Man
dialogue.text: Got it. Thanks for all your help.

groups.instructionTh: ฟังการบรรยาย/ประกาศ แล้วตอบคำถาม 5 ข้อ
groups.title: Lecture: Watching a volcano
groups.text:
Good afternoon, everyone. Last week we looked at how volcanoes form. Today I want to turn to a more practical question: how do scientists know when a volcano is about to erupt? The honest answer is that they can't know for certain. But they can watch for warning signs, and modern monitoring has become remarkably good at reading them.

The first and most important tool is the seismometer, which records small earthquakes. When magma pushes upward, it cracks the rock around it and produces swarms of tiny tremors that people on the surface usually can't feel. A sudden rise in the number of these tremors is often the earliest signal that something is changing underground.

The second sign is ground deformation. As magma collects beneath a volcano, the surface can swell slightly, a bit like a balloon being slowly blown up. The change may be only a few centimetres, so it's measured with GPS stations placed on the slopes and, more and more often, with satellites that compare images taken weeks apart.

Third, scientists measure the gases escaping from vents in the ground. A rise in sulfur dioxide, in particular, suggests that fresh magma is getting closer to the surface. Teams used to collect gas samples by hand, which was dangerous work. Today many volcanoes have automatic sensors, and some observatories even fly small drones through the gas clouds.

Now, none of these signs is reliable on its own. Earthquake swarms can fade away without any eruption at all. That's why observatories combine all three types of data before they raise an alert level. Take Mount Keralu, the volcano in your assignment data. Tremors there increased for months, but the alert level was raised only when the ground began to swell and gas readings doubled in the same week.

For Thursday, please read chapter seven and download the Keralu data set from the course website. Working in teams, you'll decide at what point you would have warned the public.

options: The history of several famous volcanic eruptions

Ways of detecting signs that an eruption may be coming
The processes by which volcanoes are formed

groups.instructionTh: ฟังการบรรยาย/ประกาศ แล้วตอบคำถาม 5 ข้อ
groups.title: Field trip briefing
groups.text:
Okay, everyone, can I have your attention for a few minutes before you go? This is the briefing for Saturday's field trip to the Pak Lan mangrove research station, so please listen carefully, because some details have changed since the email you received on Monday.

First, the departure time. The bus will now leave from the car park behind the Science Building at six-thirty, not seven as the email said. The reason is the tide. We need to reach the boardwalk while the water is still low, because that's the only time you can see the roots and the mud flats clearly. If we arrive late, we'll be looking at nothing but water.

When we get there, you'll work in pairs. Each pair will mark out a square, one metre by one metre, and count the crabs and snails inside it. Then you'll measure how deep the mud is at each corner. Please record everything on the printed data sheets, not on your phones. Last year, two pairs lost all their data when their phones got wet, and they had to borrow another group's results, which rather defeats the purpose of the exercise.

As for clothing, wear shoes you don't mind getting muddy. Sandals are not allowed on the boardwalk, because the wood can be slippery and there are sharp shells in the mud. Bring a hat, sunscreen and at least two bottles of water. Lunch will be provided by the station.

We should be back on campus at around four. Your report is due two weeks after the trip, and it should compare the results from your own square with the figures for the class as a whole.

Finally, if you can't come for any reason, let me know by Thursday so that I can offer your place to someone on the waiting list. Any questions?

items.stem: What is the main purpose of the talk?

groups.title: How children learn to talk
groups.text:
How do young children acquire their first language so quickly? By the age of four, most children can produce fairly complex sentences, ___1___ nobody has ever given them a grammar lesson. For much of the twentieth century, researchers argued about whether this ability is mainly ___2___ or mainly learned from the environment.

One influential view held that children are born with a mental framework that ___3___ them to recognise the basic patterns of any human language. Supporters of this idea pointed out that children often produce forms they have never heard, such as "goed" instead of "went." Such errors suggest that children are not simply ___4___ adults; they are actively building rules of their own.

Other researchers placed more weight on the input children receive. A long-term study known as the Linden Family Project found that children ___5___ parents spoke to them often, and in response to their interests, had larger vocabularies by the age of three. The ___6___ of talk mattered as well as the amount: back-and-forth exchanges were far more useful than speech the child merely overheard.

Today, most specialists accept that both factors play a role. Children appear to come equipped with powerful learning abilities, ___7___ these abilities need rich social interaction to develop fully. This helps explain why a child left in front of a screen ___8___ hours of foreign-language cartoons usually learns much less than one who plays with a speaker of that language for a far shorter time.

These findings have important ___9___ for teachers of second languages. Simply exposing learners to a language is rarely enough. What seems to matter most is meaningful communication, in ___10___ learners must understand and respond to real messages.

groups.title: Why bridges need gaps
groups.text:
Anyone who has walked across a long bridge may have noticed metal plates with teeth like a comb ___1___ the road at regular intervals. These are expansion joints, and without them, many bridges would slowly tear themselves apart.

The reason lies in a simple physical fact: most materials expand when they are heated and contract when they cool. A steel bridge one kilometre long can grow by ___2___ much as forty centimetres between a cold winter night and a hot summer afternoon. If the ends of the bridge were fixed rigidly in place, this movement would have nowhere to go, and the resulting stress could ___3___ the concrete or bend the steel beams out of shape.

Expansion joints solve this problem by leaving small gaps ___4___ sections of the bridge. The comb-like teeth slide past one another as each gap opens and closes, ___5___ cars and trucks to cross smoothly whatever the temperature. On smaller bridges, engineers may use a strip of rubber instead, which ___6___ and stretches as needed.

However, expansion joints are also among the weakest parts of any bridge. Because they are constantly moving and are struck by thousands of tyres every day, they ___7___ out faster than the rest of the structure. Water and road salt can leak through damaged joints and ___8___ the steel underneath. For this reason, inspectors at the Northgate Transport Authority check joints far more often than ___9___ parts of a bridge.

Some newer bridges are designed with fewer joints, relying instead on flexible supports that absorb movement. ___10___, for very long spans, the humble expansion joint remains essential.

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถาม
groups.title: Small loans, big expectations
groups.text:
In the 1970s, a small group of economists began asking a question that most banks had never taken seriously: could people with almost no money be trusted to repay a loan? Traditional banks had always assumed the answer was no. Poor households had no property to offer as security, kept no written financial records, and wanted to borrow amounts so small that processing the paperwork cost more than the interest the bank could earn. As a result, millions of farmers, street vendors and craft workers were left with two choices: save slowly for years or borrow from local moneylenders who often charged extremely high rates.

Microfinance was designed to fill this gap. Its basic idea is to offer very small loans, sometimes worth less than a week's wages in a richer country, to people who would otherwise be shut out of the financial system. Early programmes found an ingenious way to replace the security that banks normally require. Instead of lending to individuals, they lent to small groups of five or six neighbours. Each member received a loan, but if one person failed to repay, none of the others would be allowed to borrow again. This arrangement turned social ties into a kind of guarantee. Members encouraged one another, shared advice and, when necessary, helped a struggling neighbour meet a payment.

The early results were striking. Many programmes reported repayment rates above ninety-five percent, higher than those of some ordinary commercial banks. Stories spread of women who had used a tiny loan to buy a sewing machine or a few goats and gradually built a profitable business. Such stories attracted funding from governments and charities, and by the early 2000s microfinance was widely praised as one of the most promising tools for reducing poverty.

More recent research, however, has painted a more complicated picture. A series of careful studies comparing villages with and without access to microloans found that the loans did help some families cope with sudden costs and smooth out irregular incomes. Yet the average increase in household income was modest, and only a minority of borrowers actually started new businesses. In some regions, competition among lenders led people to take out several loans at once, using one to repay another, until they were deeper in debt than before.

None of this means that microfinance has failed. Rather, it suggests that the early claims were too ambitious. A small loan cannot, by itself, overcome poor roads, weak markets or a lack of training. Many organisations have therefore broadened their services, offering savings accounts, insurance and business courses alongside credit. The lesson, as development economist Amara Velasco of the Hollis Institute puts it, is that "money is a tool, not a solution."

groups.instructionTh: อ่านบทความ แล้วตอบคำถาม
groups.title: Rivers of ice
groups.text:
Glaciers look motionless, but they are in fact slow-moving rivers of ice. Formed over centuries as snow piles up faster than it melts, a glacier eventually becomes so heavy that the ice near its base begins to deform and flow downhill under its own weight. Some glaciers creep forward only a few centimetres a day; others, especially those that end in the sea, can travel several metres in the same period.

Scientists study glaciers for several reasons. One of the most practical is water supply. In many mountain regions, glaciers act like natural water towers. They store precipitation as ice during the cold season and release it gradually as meltwater during warm, dry months, precisely when farms and towns need it most. In the Talvik Valley, a high farming region studied by researchers from Norland University, nearly half of the summer river flow comes from glacier melt.

A glacier's health is usually described in terms of its mass balance: the difference between the ice it gains each year from snowfall and the ice it loses through melting and, for some glaciers, through large chunks breaking off into lakes or the sea. When gains and losses are roughly equal, the glacier stays about the same size. When losses consistently exceed gains, the glacier thins, and its front, known as the terminus, retreats up the valley.

Measuring mass balance used to require teams of researchers to hike onto the ice, drill holes and insert long poles called stakes. By returning months later and noting how much of each stake had become exposed, they could calculate how much surface ice had melted. This method is still used, but it is now supported by satellites that measure changes in the height of the ice surface and even tiny variations in the pull of gravity caused by shifting masses of ice.

These measurements reveal a troubling trend. Most mountain glaciers worldwide have been losing mass for decades, and the rate of loss has increased. In the short term, this can actually mean more water in rivers, as stored ice melts faster than usual. Researchers call the highest point of this increase "peak water." But once a glacier shrinks past a certain size, summer flow begins to decline, sometimes sharply. Communities that have grown used to a generous supply may suddenly find it shrinking just as their demand is rising.

Predicting when peak water will arrive in a particular valley is therefore one of the key questions in glacier research today. The answer depends not only on climate but also on each glacier's size, shape and altitude, which is why scientists insist that every glacier be studied on its own terms.

groups.title: Passing goods along
groups.text:
Long before container ships and cargo planes, goods moved across continents along networks of trade routes that linked peoples who never met one another. Historians sometimes picture these routes as single roads running from one end of the known world to the other. In reality, they worked more like relay races. A bale of cloth might pass through the hands of a dozen merchants, each of whom carried it only a few hundred kilometres before selling it to the next. Because no single trader travelled the whole distance, knowledge also moved in fragments. Merchants at one end of a route often had only vague ideas about where their goods finally ended up, and stories about faraway lands grew stranger with each retelling.

Geography largely determined where routes ran. Caravans crossing deserts depended on oases spaced roughly a day or two apart, since camels could go without water for some time but people and other pack animals still needed regular rest and fresh supplies. Mountain passes, which were blocked by snow for part of the year, forced traders to time their journeys carefully. At sea, the seasonal winds were decisive: ships sailed in one direction while the winds blew toward the land and waited months to return when they reversed.

These patterns gave enormous importance to the towns where routes met. Oasis settlements and port cities grew wealthy not mainly by producing goods but by providing services: water, food, storage, protection and markets where merchants from different regions could do business. Records from the Sareth Road, a desert route studied by archaeologists from the Orvane Institute, show that one oasis town charged a fee on every animal that entered its gates, and that this income paid for its walls, its wells and a large covered market.

Trade routes carried more than silk, spices and metals. Ideas, technologies and languages travelled with the merchants. Techniques for making paper, new crops and systems of counting spread along the same paths as luxury goods. Diseases did too, and some historians argue that the movement of illness along trade networks shaped history as much as the movement of wealth.

The decline of a particular route usually had several causes. When ships became able to carry larger cargoes more cheaply, some overland roads lost much of their traffic. Disputes between neighbouring states could close a route for years, pushing merchants to look for alternatives. Even changes in fashion played a part: when demand for a certain dye or perfume fell in distant markets, the towns that had grown rich by supplying it could fade within a generation.

Studying these networks reminds us that globalisation is not entirely new. The scale and speed of modern trade are unprecedented, but the basic pattern, in which distant regions depend on one another through long chains of exchange, is very old indeed.

groups.title: Reading the small print
groups.text:
Walk down any supermarket aisle and you will find packages covered in numbers: calories, grams of fat, milligrams of sodium, percentages of daily values. Nutrition labels were introduced to help shoppers make informed choices, but research suggests that many people either ignore them or misread them. Understanding why reveals as much about human psychology as it does about food.

The most common problem is serving size. The figures on a label usually describe a single serving rather than the whole package, and the serving chosen by the manufacturer may be smaller than the amount most people actually eat. A bag of crisps might list 150 calories per serving while containing three servings. A shopper who glances at the number and then finishes the bag has eaten three times what they believed. In one experiment at the Westbrook Consumer Lab, fewer than one in four participants checked the serving size before estimating the calories in a snack.

Another difficulty is the sheer amount of information. A typical label may contain more than fifteen separate figures. Faced with so much data, and often in a hurry, shoppers tend to focus on one or two numbers that they have heard are important and overlook the rest. Someone trying to cut down on sugar may choose a product that is low in sugar but high in salt without realising it.

Packaging adds a further complication. Phrases such as "light," "natural" or "made with real fruit" appear in large, colourful letters on the front of the box, while the detailed label sits in small print on the back. These front-of-pack claims can create what researchers call a "health halo": a general impression that a product is good for you, which discourages buyers from checking the details. A cereal advertised as "whole grain" may still contain a large amount of added sugar.

To address these problems, several countries have experimented with simpler designs. Some use a traffic-light system, in which red, amber and green circles show whether a product is high, medium or low in fat, sugar and salt. Others print a single summary score on the front of the package. Early evidence suggests that such systems help shoppers compare similar products quickly, although critics argue that reducing a food to one colour or one score can hide important differences between products.

In the end, no label can make decisions for us. But knowing the common traps, such as checking the serving size first, reading beyond the front of the box and looking at the whole label rather than a single number, can turn a confusing panel of figures into a genuinely useful tool.

groups.title: Robots in the field
groups.text:
For most of history, farming has depended on large amounts of human labour. Even after tractors and combine harvesters transformed agriculture in the twentieth century, many tasks remained stubbornly manual. Picking soft fruit, removing weeds between rows of vegetables and checking individual plants for disease all required human eyes and hands. Today, a new generation of agricultural robots is beginning to take on these jobs, and the change may reshape rural life as profoundly as the tractor once did.

Unlike earlier farm machines, which were large and powerful, many of these robots are small, light and highly specialised. One type, now being tested on vegetable farms, moves slowly along crop rows, using cameras and software to tell the difference between a lettuce seedling and a weed. When it spots a weed, it removes it with a tiny blade or a precise burst of heat. Because it targets individual plants, it can greatly reduce the need for chemical weedkillers sprayed across whole fields.

Fruit picking has proved more difficult. A strawberry or a tomato must be located among the leaves, judged to be ripe and then gripped firmly enough to be pulled off but gently enough not to be bruised. Engineers at Calder Robotics, a start-up working with growers in the Brennan Hills region, spent four years developing a soft gripper modelled on the human hand. Their latest prototype picks around 1,800 strawberries an hour, roughly the same as an experienced worker, although it still struggles with fruit hidden deep inside the plant.

Supporters argue that robots could solve a pressing problem. In many countries, farms find it increasingly hard to hire seasonal workers, and crops sometimes rot in the fields because there is no one to harvest them. Robots can work at night and do not get tired. In addition, the detailed data they collect on the size, health and ripeness of every plant could help farmers use water and fertiliser more efficiently.

Yet there are reasons for caution. The machines are expensive, and small family farms may be unable to afford them, which could widen the gap between large agricultural businesses and everyone else. Robots also require reliable internet connections and skilled technicians, both of which are scarce in many rural areas. Finally, there is the question of what will happen to workers whose jobs disappear. Some experts believe that new roles in maintenance and data analysis will be created, while others doubt that these will be numerous enough, or located in the right places, to replace the jobs that are lost.

Agricultural robots are unlikely to replace human farmers entirely in the near future. More probably, they will become one more tool, like the tractor, that changes what farm work looks like and who does it.

items.explanationTh: วลี "along with her assistants" ไม่นับรวมเป็นประธาน ประธานจริงคือ "The professor" กริยาจึงต้องเป็น "is preparing"

groups.instructionTh: เลือกส่วนที่ขีดเส้นใต้ (A, B, C หรือ D) ที่ไม่ถูกต้องตามหลักไวยากรณ์

items.stem: Trade routes [[enabled]] not only goods [[but also]] ideas [[spreading]] [[across]] continents.
items.explanationTh: "enable + กรรม + to + V1" ต้องเป็น "to spread" ไม่ใช่ spreading

items.stem: If the observatory [[had raised]] the alert earlier, more residents [[would leave]] the area [[before]] the ash cloud [[reached]] the town.
items.explanationTh: ประโยคเงื่อนไขแบบที่ 3 พูดถึงอดีตที่ไม่เกิดขึ้นจริง (If + had raised) ส่วนผลต้องเป็น "would have left" ไม่ใช่ would leave

items.stem: Shoppers [[compare]] prices far more carefully [[for]] the past two years, [[according to]] a survey [[carried out]] by the Westbrook Consumer Lab.
items.explanationTh: "for the past two years" แสดงการกระทำที่ต่อเนื่องจากอดีตถึงปัจจุบัน กริยาต้องเป็น present perfect "have compared"

items.stem: Many economists [[argue]] [[that]] microfinance works best [[when]] [[combining]] with training programmes.
items.explanationTh: microfinance เป็นฝ่ายถูกนำไปรวม จึงต้องใช้รูป passive "when combined with" ไม่ใช่ combining

items.stem: The survey [[was]] [[conducting]] by a team [[of]] graduate students [[from]] three universities.
items.explanationTh: มี "by a team" แสดงว่าเป็น passive ต้องใช้ "was conducted"

items.stem: [[Unlike]] earlier machines, [[modern]] farm robots are small, light and [[high]] [[specialised]].
items.explanationTh: คำที่ขยายคุณศัพท์ "specialised" ต้องเป็นกริยาวิเศษณ์ "highly"

items.stem: The course aims to improve students' ability [[to read]] academic texts, [[writing]] clear summaries, and [[to present]] their findings [[confidently]].
items.explanationTh: โครงสร้างคู่ขนาน to read ..., to write ..., and to present ... ต้องใช้รูปเดียวกัน จึงต้องเป็น "to write" ไม่ใช่ writing

items.stem: The dormitory manager insisted [[on]] [[inspect]] every room [[before]] the [[semester]] ended.
items.explanationTh: หลังบุพบท "insist on" ต้องใช้ V-ing คือ "insisted on inspecting"

items.stem: [[Because of]] the leak [[had]] damaged the wiring, the technician [[turned off]] the power [[immediately]].
items.explanationTh: ตามด้วยอนุประโยค (ประธาน + กริยา "the leak had damaged") ต้องใช้ "Because" ส่วน because of ตามด้วยคำนามเท่านั้น

items.stem: [[The amount of]] volunteers who [[signed up]] for the survey [[was]] far [[higher]] than the organisers had expected.
items.explanationTh: "volunteers" เป็นคำนามนับได้ ต้องใช้ "The number of" ส่วน the amount of ใช้กับคำนามนับไม่ได้ (กริยา was ถูกแล้วเพราะ the number of ถือเป็นเอกพจน์)
